findings.title: Relay treats knowledge of tokenHash as machine identity — no proof-of-possession of the raw token at /control
findings.failure_scenario: handleRegister authenticates a machine by tokenHash alone. Anyone who learns a machine's sha256(token) (the only value the relay persists in state.json) can register as that machine's id, or re-pair the hash away from a currently-offline legitimate machine (lines 192-203 explicitly delete the offline twin), then receive {t:'conn'} knocks and open /tunnel legs. They still cannot answer the phone's handshake (the home gateway would 401), but they occupy the machine slot, receive connection metadata, and can blackhole/DoS the pairing; combined with C-02's raw-token exposure paths any hash leak becomes a full machine-takeover primitive.
findings.preconditions: Attacker has read access to the relay state file (/root/.moch/relay-service/state.json on the VPS — root compromise, backup leak, or misconfigured perms) or any other hash disclosure, plus network reachability to /control. The legitimate machine must be offline for the takeover path (line 197 refuses a live holder).
evidence: relay/moch-relay-server.js:183-190 — registration validates only id shape, tokenHash shape, optional relay key; never the raw token
relay/moch-relay-server.js:192-203 — offline twin holding the same tokenHash is deleted ('re-pairing token hash from offline machine')
relay/moch-relay-server.js:146 — state.json reload restores tokenHash as the sole credential
reproduction_steps: On any host, open ws /control to the relay
Send {t:'register', machine:'m-x', tokenHash:<hash read from state.json>} — accepted unless the hash holder is live
Phone dials /api/ws?token=<real token>; relay routes the conn to the attacker's socket
findings.suggested_remediation: Require the raw token (or an HMAC over a server nonce) at /control registration, exactly as /tunnel already does; keep only the hash at rest.
findings.limitations: Did not verify deployed VPS state.json permissions (out of scope, no network). Severity assumes hash confidentiality is the only barrier today.

findings.title: Raw pairing token travels in relay URL query strings on both legs — lands in reverse-proxy access logs; 'relay never sees the token' comment is false
findings.failure_scenario: The phone dials /api/ws?token=<raw pairing token> (app/src/lib/gateway.ts:149); the relay reads the raw token and hashes it locally (line 312), and moch-tunnel dials /tunnel/<id>?key=<raw token> (moch-link/install.sh:223). TLS terminates at nginx on the VPS, so the relay operator (and anyone reading nginx access logs, which by default log the full query string) obtains the raw gateway pairing token. That token IS the full session credential: with it one can dial /api/ws directly and drive the user's entire hermes gateway (sessions, transcripts, file r/w, exec approval flow) whenever the home machine is online. The header comments at relay:9-12 and install.sh:40-44 ('the relay never sees the pairing token, only its sha256') are incorrect.
findings.preconditions: Position: any reader of VPS logs (nginx access.log, journal) or the relay process memory/operator. No exploit needed — standing exposure by design of the URL transport.
evidence: relay/moch-relay-server.js:308-312 — token taken from url.searchParams.get('token') before hashing
relay/moch-relay-server.js:377-381 — /tunnel?key=<raw token>
app/src/lib/gateway.ts:148-149 — token embedded in the WS dial URL (query string, not header)
app/src/lib/push.ts advertisement: push token also on the query string (gateway.ts:158)
moch-link/install.sh:222-223 — raw token as the tunnel-leg key in a URL
reproduction_steps: nginx on the relay VPS logs GET /api/ws?token=… verbatim (default log format)
grep the access log → recover the pairing token → dial wss://api.moch.softland.tech/api/ws?token=… and speak JSON-RPC as the user
findings.suggested_remediation: Move the phone token to the X-Hermes-Session-Token header (already supported by the relay, line 305-309, and by the app's REST path) and have the WS client send it in a header too; send the tunnel key in a header as well. Fix the misleading comments.
findings.limitations: Actual nginx log config not in repo — retention/disk exposure is an assumption of default config; mechanism (query-string transport) is fully traced.

findings.title: Relay registration is open by default; unauthenticated /control sockets have no lifecycle cap
findings.failure_scenario: --require-key defaults to empty (line 61), so any internet host that can reach the relay port may register up to --max-machines-per-ip (20) machines with arbitrary ids and arbitrary tokenHashes. Registration is permanent (persisted to state.json), enabling: (a) state.json pollution/persistence on the VPS; (b) socket-flooding /control before register — sockets that never register get no heartbeat and no timeout, so idle connections hold server resources indefinitely; (c) /health (line 433) leaks online-machine and live-connection counts unauthenticated. A remote attacker cannot evict another IP's machines (eviction at lines 217-227 is same-IP only), so impact is abuse-of-service and reconnaissance, not session hijack.
findings.preconditions: Network reachability to the relay port. PROJECT.md puts the relay behind nginx on api.moch.softland.tech; if the raw port (9591) is firewalled and nginx only proxies specific paths, exposure shrinks accordingly — config not in repo.
evidence: relay/moch-relay-server.js:61 — requireKey: '' default
relay/moch-relay-server.js:183-266 — no auth path when requireKey empty
relay/moch-relay-server.js:268-287 — connection handler sets no idle timeout for never-registering sockets
relay/moch-relay-server.js:433-436 — unauthenticated /health returns counts
relay/moch-relay-server.js:498 — server.listen(cfg.port) binds all interfaces (no host arg)
reproduction_steps: Open N idle /control WebSocket connections; send nothing — none are ever reaped
Register 20 machines with random hashes from one IP; they persist across restarts via state.json
findings.suggested_remediation: Default --require-key on (or auto-generate a key at deploy), add a register-timeout for unauthenticated control sockets, and gate /health counts behind the key.
findings.limitations: Cannot verify live firewall/nginx path filtering from the repo.

findings.title: Release builds silently fall back to the publicly tracked debug.keystore; the keystore itself is committed
findings.failure_scenario: signingConfigs.release is populated only when keystore.properties exists (gitignored); otherwise buildTypes.release signs with signingConfigs.debug, whose keystore is tracked in the repo at app/android/app/debug.keystore with the universal 'android' passwords. PROJECT.md documents local ./gradlew assembleRelease as the routine test path, and the GitHub-hosted v1.0.0 APK predates the EAS flow. If any distributed APK is signed with this key, anyone with the repo can build a malicious 'update' that Android installs over it (same signature → silent upgrade path with all permissions, including RECORD_AUDIO, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, and the embedded agent runtime).
findings.preconditions: A released/sideloaded APK actually signed by the debug key (v1.0.0 release signing not verifiable in-repo), plus attacker knowledge of the repo (public).
evidence: app/android/app/build.gradle — release block: signingConfig keystorePropertiesFile.exists() ? signingConfigs.release : signingConfigs.debug
git ls-files — app/android/app/debug.keystore is tracked; passwords 'android' hardcoded in build.gradle
PROJECT.md:82-85 — local gradle release builds are the norm for testing
reproduction_steps: git clone the repo; assembleRelease with no keystore.properties → APK signed with the committed key
If a published APK shares that signature, adb install -r the malicious APK upgrades it in place
findings.suggested_remediation: Make release builds fail (not fall back) when keystore.properties is absent; remove debug.keystore from git or accept it for debug variant only.
findings.limitations: Confidence medium because harm requires a debug-signed distributed build; no APK artifact was inspected.

findings.title: usesCleartextTraffic=true app-wide, and pairing links default tls=0 — a crafted hermes://connect QR silently dials plaintext ws to a remote host with the token in the URL
findings.failure_scenario: The manifest allows cleartext for the whole app. Pairing defaults to tls=false whenever the tls parameter is absent or not '1' (app/src/lib/pairing.ts:37-41), and the only guard for a non-local plaintext dial is a log warning (app/src/lib/gateway.ts:559-561) plus an unencrypted fetch path (http.ts:5). A malicious or mistyped pairing QR/link therefore pairs a remote host over plaintext — token and the entire chat stream (provider-key-gated model output, file contents, exec approvals) are readable by any on-path listener.
findings.preconditions: User scans/accepts a pairing link whose host is off-device and tls omitted; attacker positioned on the network path (or running the named host).
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:23 — android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"
app/src/lib/pairing.ts:37 — tlsRaw default '0'
app/src/lib/gateway.ts:559-561 — warn-only for plain ws:// to non-local host
app/src/lib/http.ts:5 — httpBase mirrors tls=false to http://
reproduction_steps: Craft hermes://connect?host=<remote>&token=t (no tls param) as a QR
Victim scans and connects in a café Wi-Fi; attacker sniffs the ws frames and the token
findings.suggested_remediation: Default tls=1 for non-private addresses, or require an explicit user confirmation dialog before any non-local plaintext dial; scope cleartext to 127.0.0.1 via networkSecurityConfig.
findings.limitations: Social-engineering precondition; no on-device test performed.

findings.title: WebView debugging enabled process-wide in release builds — resident agent WebView holds browsing session, cookies readable over adb
findings.failure_scenario: AgentBrowserHost mounts an always-alive WebView with webviewDebuggingEnabled (and BrowserRelayModule.kt:117-123 calls WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled, documented there as process-wide). Functionally required for the CdpRelay/CDP toolchain, but release builds ship with WebView debugging on for EVERY WebView. Anyone with brief USB/adb access to the phone attaches chrome://inspect to the agent WebView and the gateway dashboard WebView and extracts cookies, logins, and page content — browserRelay.ts notes logins live in the WebView profile.
findings.preconditions: Physical/adb access to the unlocked device (or a compromised adb chain). No root needed.
evidence: app/src/components/AgentBrowserHost.tsx:53 — webviewDebuggingEnabled on the permanent offscreen WebView
app/android/.../BrowserRelayModule.kt:22,117-123 — process-wide setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)
app/src/lib/browserRelay.ts:19 — 'logins live in the WebView profile (CookieManager)'
reproduction_steps: Enable developer options/USB debugging, attach Chrome DevTools, select the Moch WebView, read cookies/storage
findings.suggested_remediation: Gate setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled on BuildConfig.DEBUG when possible, or document the trade-off; consider a separate, non-debuggable WebView for any authenticated surface.
findings.limitations: Design tension with the CDP feature acknowledged in BUILD-PLAN; no device test run.

findings.title: Executable bootstrap artifacts (proot loader .deb, Ubuntu rootfs, QR renderer) downloaded with no checksum pinning
findings.failure_scenario: First Linux bootstrap downloads proot_*.deb and libtalloc .deb from the Termux repo and the ubuntu-base tar.gz from cdimage.ubuntu.com over TLS, but verifies no hash (_download, linux_env.py:379, streams straight to disk; the stamp records only the URL). A compromised upstream, repo mirror, or any TLS-bypassing middlebox with a trusted CA yields arbitrary code: proot's loader is exec'd (via linker64) inside the app's UID on every guest command, and a malicious rootfs plants files the agent then executes. Same pattern in moch-link/install.sh:22,1044 — qrcodegen.py is fetched from raw.githubusercontent pinned only by commit hash.
findings.preconditions: Attacker controls the package repo/CDN response or holds a CA trusted by the device, at the moment of first bootstrap (or a pin change, which wipes and re-downloads, linux_env.py:519-528).
evidence: app/python-runtime/moch/linux_env.py:37,43,52 — TERMUX_BASE/PROOT_URL/ROOTFS_URLS, no sha256 anywhere in the file (grep: zero hashlib/checksum hits)
app/python-runtime/moch/linux_env.py:379-391 — _download writes bytes with no verification
moch-link/install.sh:22,1043-1044 — VENDOR_URL commit-pinned, curl -fsSL, no checksum
mitigating: _safe_extract/_check_member (linux_env.py:300-346) blocks path traversal and relative-symlink escapes in the rootfs
reproduction_steps: Serve a modified proot_*.deb at the pinned URL (or intercept TLS)
Victim runs Linux bootstrap; the swapped binary is chmod 0755 and exec'd per guest command inside the app UID
findings.suggested_remediation: Pin sha256 for the proot/libtalloc debs and the rootfs tarball; publish checksums for qrcodegen.py alongside the installer.
findings.limitations: Standard supply-chain exposure; likelihood depends on upstream compromise, not app-side flaws.

findings.title: docs/install.sh (the publicly served copy) has diverged from canonical moch-link/install.sh
findings.failure_scenario: The two installer copies differ by ~430 lines: docs/install.sh ships the OLD moch-link-proxy (plain host-rewrite only) while moch-link/install.sh embeds the push-watcher/receipt proxy and all later fixes; PROJECT.md:70-73 mandates 'Always cmp the copies'. Users installing from the website get the stale tunnel/proxy behavior, and future security fixes applied only to the canonical copy will silently miss the public one.
findings.preconditions: Any user following the website install path (https://moch.softland.tech/install.sh).
evidence: diff moch-link/install.sh docs/install.sh — large divergence starting at the proxy heredoc
PROJECT.md:70-73 — sync rule explicitly requires cmp
findings.suggested_remediation: Re-copy canonical → docs (and VPS), or make docs/install.sh a build artifact of moch-link/install.sh in CI.
findings.limitations: No functional security defect in the old copy found on read; the risk is drift, not a current vuln.

findings.title: CdpRelay loopback token compared with non-constant-time !=; token is 128-bit random and loopback-only
findings.failure_scenario: segs.firstOrNull() != token is timing-sensitive, but the token is a fresh 122-bit UUID, the listener binds 127.0.0.1 only, and a cross-app timing oracle over loopback with a single boolean check is not practically exploitable at this entropy. The relay itself uses crypto.timingSafeEqual correctly (relay:98-102,190,381). Hardening note.
findings.preconditions: Another on-device app able to open many loopback connections and measure sub-microsecond timing differences — no realistic recovery path.
evidence: CdpRelay.kt:92-95 — 127.0.0.1 literal bind (BUG-106 note)
CdpRelay.kt:167 — UUID.randomUUID token
CdpRelay.kt:201 — plain string != for auth
findings.suggested_remediation: MessageDigest.isEqual(byte[], byte[]) if touched again; otherwise leave.

findings.title: Secret-file hygiene verified clean on the tracked-tree side; debug keystore + google-services.json are the only committed credential-adjacent files
findings.failure_scenario: Verified without printing contents: root firebase-service-account.json exists UNTRACKED and gitignored (mode 0600) with zero commit history — the admin credential never entered git. Root google-services.json and app/android/app/google-services.json are tracked — normal Firebase client config (identifiers, not secrets), root copy redundant. debug.keystore tracked (see C-04). SecureStore primary with AsyncStorage fallback now logs a warning (gateway.ts:206-215, known BUG-071); logs scrubbed via redactedUrl (gateway.ts:163-166); log.ts mirrors to console only in __DEV__. allowBackup=true with expo-secure-store rules — plaintext-AsyncStorage-fallback tokens WOULD ride device backups.
evidence: .gitignore:6 — firebase-service-account.json ignored; mode 0600; zero git history
git ls-files — google-services.json x2 and debug.keystore tracked
app/src/lib/gateway.ts:163-166,206-215 — redaction + warned plaintext fallback (BUG-071)
relay state: machines Map persists tokenHash only (relay:157-171)
findings.suggested_remediation: Drop the redundant root google-services.json from tracking if unused; keep firebase-service-account.json untracked and consider moving it out of the repo dir entirely.
findings.limitations: Contents of secret files intentionally not read beyond existence/mode/tracking.

notes_for_parent: Overlaps deliberately NOT re-filed: BUG-120 (confirmed still accurate in gateway_server.py) and BUG-071. Amplification for BUG-120 triage: the leaked token reaches the full embedded surface — gateway RPC -> HermesBridge -> linux_session.run()/terminal.write() (agent-controlled guest shell over proot; binds of /dev, /proc, workspace, scratch only; no /system or /data bind) — practical impact is guest-shell access inside app-private storage, not just transcript reads. No RCE-beyond-app-UID path found in Moch-authored code; guest exec is same-UID by design (proot is ptrace path-rewriting, not a sandbox).
